Partially resolved 2026-09-11. The malformed row gives 0.29 with the W missing from the dimensional unit; 0.29 W/(m-K) is within the published range for unfilled PEEK (~0.25-0.29), so the reading is plausible - but it is an inference from the literature, not the source, so no conductivity is normalized. PEEK is outside the H2C envelope, so this is low priority. Action: request the ISO 22007 report or a corrected TDS.

Resolved as non-blocking 2026-09-11. The H2C hardware baseline is 350 C nozzle / 120 C bed / 65 C chamber (Method H2C row; confirmed on the Bambu H2C specification page). Every published 3DXTECH PEEK range exceeds it - the current TDS printed-specimen block gives 380-400 C nozzle and 130-140 C bed, and both previously recorded ranges (360-450/120-160 and 400-480/140-180) are also out of envelope. The conflict therefore cannot change the exclusion, and both ranges are retained without reconciliation.

PEEK is a very difficult material to 3D print.
Your printer should have adequate thermal control in the build chamber throughout the printing process.
Lack of process control can also lead to speccing on the part with black specs forming during printing on your part.
Lack of process control and inadequate temperatures can also lead to brown discoloration in the part, which is an indication that the parts has not been properly crystalized.
Do not let the PEEK material remain in your printer's nozzle for extended periods of time when not extruding.

You could post 3D printing anneal your PEEK part in an oven.
